attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'appears', so it is a claim about the visible record, not a probability hedge. It also keeps the 'unlimited capital' qualifier.

contract.note: Reading 'actually makes a profit' as GAAP profit is fair and ordinary. Leaving out diversified hyperscalers and limiting the check to the record up to the post date fits 'appears'. The GAAP-versus-adjusted choice matters, because Anthropic's adjusted profit came later.

evidence.note: Per its S-1, Anthropic had an $8.06B GAAP operating loss in 2025. That period falls inside the target window and the item was available before the evaluation date.
OpenAI's Q1 2026 operating loss was $9.3B, from shareholder documents as reported by The Information. Unaudited, but it is a company-reported figure for the period.
Anthropic's Q2 2026 operating profit is for a quarter that ended after the post. The same item says it was the only profitable quarter, so Q1 2026 was a loss.
Before the post, Anthropic's profit was only a projection given to investors, not a reported result.

reviews.rationale: As of the post, the two leading AI-model sellers had only reported GAAP losses: Anthropic for 2025 and every quarter before Q2 2026, and OpenAI for Q1 2026. Anthropic's first operating profit came in a quarter that ended after the post. 'Nobody' was checked only against the main providers, which is what the contract's support condition asks, and the hedge 'appears' fits that scope.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the absolute claim and the contract-role exception. It leaves out 'we can't measure AI job loss', but the contract covers that point.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary. Splitting the claim into an absolute part (no replacement) and a softer part (no broad measurable loss) is fair. The result depends on whether CEO accounts and correlational studies count as replacement.

evidence.note: Salesforce's CEO says support headcount fell from about 9k to about 5k because AI agents took over the work (Aug 2025). This is a company disclosure, not independently checked.
A Stanford payroll study measures a 13% relative employment decline for early-career workers in AI-exposed jobs. It is correlational.
The Yale Budget Lab finds no economy-wide labor disruption, which backs the softer point.
Oxford Economics suggests some layoffs blamed on AI are AI-washing. This weakens CEO accounts but does not refute Salesforce's.
Block's cuts are tied partly to AI and partly to overhiring, so they do not clearly show AI doing the work.

reviews.rationale: The softer part holds: aggregate data (Yale) show no economy-wide AI displacement. The absolute part, that AI does not replace jobs and its job loss can't be measured, is contradicted under the contract. Salesforce reports cutting support staff because AI agents took over the work, and the Stanford study measures employment declines tied to AI exposure, though both have caveats.
